5.3.1 Crisis Profiles

Pandemics. Pandemic research centered on Chronic Strains (15 items), the prolonged uncertainty of a crisis, rather than the discrete shocks of Life Events (3). Anxiety, depression, and perceived stress, the outcomes most often modeled, likewise track sustained strain rather than a single traumatic event.

Lockdowns and frontline duty disrupted routines, work, health, and help seeking at once. Pandemic studies accordingly supplied 12 of 19 Coping items, 14 of 29 Cumulative Physiological Burden items, 6 of 11 Health Behaviors, and 6 of 14 Occupation items. Distancing strained social ties: 5 Bridging Social Capital items covered loneliness and online support, and 5 Bonding items captured family problems and support. Mastery & Self Concept (10 items) was the main favorable construct, linked to lower anxiety and depression.

Armed conflicts. Of the 35 Life Events items, 23 came from armed conflict research. So did 12 of the 16 previous-outcome and previous-symptom items, all of them adverse. Two studies linked these items to PTSD and suicidal ideation, the most common outcomes in this crisis type. Trauma exposure thus recurred with prior psychiatric history and 13 Cumulative Physiological Burden items, such as previous injuries. This pattern is consistent with negative outcomes accumulating on prior vulnerability.

Mastery & Self Concept items, such as hopelessness, were also prominent, as were social capital items, such as unit cohesion and family contact. Insecurity, fear, and discrimination made up 6 Chronic Strains items, and all 5 Coping items were maladaptive, such as avoidance and alcohol misuse. These items were adverse, consistent with the PTSD and suicidal ideation.

Natural-hazard disasters. Natural-hazard disaster research shared the trauma focus of armed conflicts and its outcomes centered on probable PTSD. Likewise, its 9 Life Events items included hurricane exposure and observing flames, mostly linked to PTSD. Housing loss is a physical consequence of disasters, not of public health restrictions or economic contractions, so 12 of the 14 Housing items came from this research.

Adverse items linked to harmful outcomes like PTSD included property loss, and bereavement, with 5 Bonding Social Capital items recording lost relatives or living alone. Contextual & Environmental Conditions (6 items) captured the hazard itself, such as wildfire events, temperature, and precipitation.

Economic upheavals. Studies of economic upheaval modeled depression, distress, and suicide mortality. All 9 of its Occupation, Income, and Financial Means items were adverse, pointing to job and income loss as the defining harm. Chronic Strains and Mastery & Self Concept were equally common (4 items each), reflecting work-life conflict, exhaustion, and a shaken sense of control. Age was adverse in both studies that coded it, as younger adults fared worse.

5.3.2 Computational Method Profiles

The data source determined which determinants studies could detect. Text-based methods supplied 56 of the 312 coded items, including 19 of the 66 structural items (29%), against 15% in the other two dimensions. They detected 6 of 8 Governance and 4 of 9 Contextual & Environmental Conditions items, which predicted stress or distress. Text also yielded 6 of 14 Occupation items, half of them concerning suicide. It supplied 7 of 28 Mastery & Self Concept items, tied to wellbeing, and 9 of 30 Chronic Strains items, tied to depression or stress. Public text, such as social media posts, likely discusses policies, restrictions, and employment more readily than surveys do.

The other 52 studies drew on surveys, clinical instruments, or administrative records. They supplied 256 of the 312 coded items and remained the primary source as NLP grew. Because they ask about individual exposure, symptoms, and resources, most of their items were intermediary and modeled depression, PTSD, or anxiety. They supplied 21 of 28 Mastery & Self Concept and 21 of 30 Chronic Strains items, and trauma checklists 32 of 35 Life Events items, chiefly for PTSD. Structured questionnaires also recorded all 10 Age and 9 Gender items, demographics that public text rarely reports. In armed conflict research they were the only source, supplying the prior psychiatric history of conflict cohorts.

5.4 RQ4: Gaps and Research Agenda

5.4.1 Research Gaps

Economic upheaval was the least studied crisis type with only 5 studies, and its occupational and financial items were all adverse (Section 5.3). The gap therefore leaves a consistent risk signal understudied. No armed conflict study utilized NLP techniques or contributed Governance or Contextual & Environmental Conditions items, even though surveys are difficult to field in conflict zones. Social media and other text sources could fill this gap. For example, Nemkova, Ubani, Polat, Kim, and Nielsen (2023) used large language models (LLMs) to detect human rights violations in social media text from the Russia-Ukraine war.

Text-based studies were few. The 11 that analyzed text supplied 56 of the 312 coded items, including 29% of structural items but 15% of items in the other two dimensions. This suggests that NLP may suit the tracking of governance, policy, and employment conditions (Section 5.3). Yet 11 studies are too few to tell whether this reflects a strength of text or an artifact of crisis type. Until more studies accrue, the strengths of NLP in crisis mental health research remain suggested rather than established.

Favorable codes clustered in a few psychosocial resources and families (Section 5.1.2). Part of this imbalance is conceptual: Mastery & Self Concept is favorable by construction. By contrast, a physiological burden, diagnosed illness, or biomarker abnormality has little scope to be recorded as positive. Surveillance that detects only risk cannot show where support is working. Only a handful measured protective constructs explicitly, as Papini et al. (2023) did with unit cohesion and Keller et al. (2026) with family contact. Only 14 of the 63 studies used a dedicated explanable AI method, 9 with SHAP values and 5 with only permutation importance (Table 1). Most of the others relied on a model's built-in importance scores. These show that a feature mattered but whether it raised or lowered distress had to be inferred (Lundberg & Lee, 2017). Methods such as SHAP report both the size and the direction of each feature's effect. Their wider use would make computational findings easier to compare across studies and with earlier reviews.

5.4.2 Research Agenda

Longitudinal cohorts and text about job loss and debt could extend coverage of economic upheaval, as Ananthasubramaniam et al. (2024) did with suicide narratives. Applying NLP to conflict-era text could add the governance and environmental constructs that conflict surveys omit. Protective constructs also deserve explicit measurement.

In armed conflict research, prior psychiatric history and physical health recurred as adverse features (Section 5.3). They supplied 12 of the 16 previous-outcome and previous-symptom items and 11 Cumulative Physiological Burden items. Because such records often already exist in health or survey data, they could act as detectors of adverse outcomes faster than traditional methods.

Digital phenotyping (Onnela & Rauch, 2016) can track behavioral and mental health signals, such as movement, screen time, and sleep, through passively collected data. It could allow continuous monitoring of chronic strains and health behaviors without repeated surveys, in conflict zones and disaster settings where survey access is often constrained. Large language models (LLMs) may also detect the less standardized language associated with these constructs. Rathje et al. (2024) found that generative pre-trained transformer models outperformed dictionary-based methods in detecting psychological constructs across languages. Thus, LLMs could help detect protective constructs and psychosocial circumstances in text-based data, which are under-represented in the current evidence base.

Knowledge graph-LLM approaches offer a way to link these data sources to the taxonomy. Pan et al. (2024) proposed using an LLM to populate graph entities and relations from unstructured text, such as clinical notes or mined discourse. Gao et al. (2025) combined a knowledge graph built from the Unified Medical Language System with an LLM to improve diagnostic prediction from electronic health record data. Their model retrieved patient-specific knowledge paths for each prediction. A similar approach would turn the taxonomy developed here into an updatable structure rather than a fixed classification.

Finally, we recommended the use of explainable AI methods to improve the interpretability of the models. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP), for example, assigns each feature a signed contribution to every prediction. A newly detected feature could thus enter the taxonomy with both its importance and its direction of association.

5.5 Limitations Selection and extraction.

One of our criteria for inclusion was that a study ranked its features on any analytical basis, or reported six or fewer features. The evidence base, therefore, favors studies that publish ranked features. Lower-ranked determinants are invisible to the prominence counts. Our dual-coded extraction process reduces coding error but does not eliminate it completely.

Evidence. Also, we did not appraise study quality or grade certainty. So the summary weights stronger and weaker studies equally, and the direction of any resulting bias is unknown. The 11 text-based studies drew mainly on Twitter, Reddit, Weibo, and YouTube. These platforms capture people with internet access and digital literacy, and under-represent older or lower-income groups at higher risk during crises. Low-and middle-income settings supplied 19 of the 63 studies and economic upheaval 5, so findings for pandemics, natural-hazard disasters, and economic upheaval rest mainly on high-income populations.

Summarizing. A construct's prominence counts how often studies reported it as influential, not its effect size, and the 47 ranking procedures produced scores that cannot be compared across studies. Only 225 of the 312 items fit a named family, so family counts are lower bounds. Tallying by direction treats a mixed code as one class, which hides how the direction varied within a study.

6 Conclusions

Computational crisis research mostly identifies risk. Most constructs pointed toward poorer mental health, and the nearly balanced ones turned on whether a resource was present or missing. These directions describe how models ranked features, not causal effects. The prominent factors largely confirmed earlier reviews, with no named risk factor reversed and age and sex among those with mixed direction. Food insecurity, national identity, and home-based work were the only families without an earlier counterpart. Because studies ranked features on incomparable scales, prominence here tracks how often a factor recurs rather than how strongly it acts.

Determinants varied with both crisis type and data source. Text-based studies reached proportionally more structural determinants, whereas surveys supplied demographics, clinical outcomes, and all armed conflict evidence. No conflict study analyzed text, so part of this method contrast may reflect crisis type instead. Coverage was thinnest for economic upheaval, protective constructs, low-and middle-income settings, and text-based study of armed conflict. Few studies used a dedicated explanation method, so most reported direction in ways that cannot be compared.

The central open challenge is timing. Current models mostly register constructs once distress has already left a clinical or administrative record. Large language models will likely extend text-based detection to protective constructs and conflict-era discourse, where dictionary methods have fallen short. Digital phenotyping should make chronic strain observable where surveys cannot reach. As explainable AI becomes routine, each new feature will enter the evidence base with its direction attached. The taxonomy and factor families give that growing evidence a shared structure, showing surveillance designers which determinants a system covers and which it leaves unobserved.

Data Availability

All included studies are published and cited in the reference list. Materials availability is not applicable, as no physical materials or reagents were used. The Zenodo deposit (Ridwan Bin Monjur, 2026) openly holds the data behind the result tables. It contains the search and screening records, every screening decision with its kappa reconciliation, and the full feature extraction and CSDH coding. Supplementary Tables 1 and 3 give the search strings and the included studies.
